analysis.one_liner: Sets federal patient-protection standards for managed care, including fast appeals, emergency care access, and mastectomy coverage.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan managed-care patient-protection bill sponsored by a Republican senator and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in July 1998 died there without a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended on January 3, 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written a federal 'patients' bill of rights' into the laws governing employer health plans and health insurers. It required plans to make fast coverage decisions, run fair internal and independent external appeals, cover emergency care, let patients see specialists and OB-GYNs directly, ban gag rules punishing doctors who advocate for patients, and guarantee hospital stays and reconstruction after mastectomies. It also added federal enforcement penalties and let patients recover economic losses from botched coverage decisions. The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of people in managed care plans and employer health coverage: patients denied care would get speedy decisions and an independent outside reviewer whose ruling binds the plan; women would get guaranteed hospital stays and reconstruction after mastectomies; doctors would be protected from retaliation for advocating for patients; and consumers would get plain-language information about what plans cover and how they pay their doctors.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients in managed care and employer plans

how_it_helps.text: Plans must make coverage decisions within 14 days — 72 hours when a delay could seriously jeopardize health — and treat a missed deadline as an appealable denial [S3].

Patients who lose an internal appeal can have the case reviewed by an independent external appeal entity with no conflict of interest, at the plan's expense, and the decision is final and binding on the plan [S3].
The bill requires coverage of emergency services, direct access to OB-GYNs and specialists, and an appropriate hospital stay plus reconstructive surgery after mastectomies [S2].

It bars plans from penalizing doctors for advocating for their patients, from transferring liability to providers through contracts, and from incentive plans that reward denying care; it also creates independent Health Insurance Ombudsmen to help consumers [S2, S3].
Federal agencies gain enforcement power to fine violations, and people responsible for untimely or improper coverage determinations become liable for the patient's economic loss [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers that sponsor plans bear compliance costs: they pay for external reviews, build new appeal and disclosure systems, and face federal penalties and liability for improper denials. Those costs would likely show up partly in premiums.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employers sponsoring plans

drawbacks.text: Compliance and external-review costs fall on plans and employers, and some of that cost would be passed to workers and small employers through higher premiums — a real trade-off an honest supporter must weigh.

The bill layers new federal requirements on top of state insurance regulation and does not fully resolve how the three agencies (HHS, Labor, Treasury) would coordinate enforcement, creating administrative complexity for plans and regulators alike [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections address problems that affected nearly every insured American in 1998 — opaque denials, slow reviews, gagged doctors — and give denied patients a genuinely independent reviewer whose decision binds the plan. The costs are real but modest relative to the stakes: faster appeals, mandatory disclosure, and liability for bad-faith denials. A well-designed bill for patients, with the main question being premium cost rather than benefit erosion.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John Chafee introduced the bill on July 31, 1998, joined by Senators Graham, Lieberman, Specter, and Baucus [S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance on July 31, 1998 [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the bill's history before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, managed care companies, and employers sponsoring health plans are better off because the bill died: they avoided new federal mandates, mandatory external review, disclosure requirements, and liability for improper coverage denials. Patients whose denials might have been overturned kept the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and employers with plans

for.name: Sen. John H. Chafee
for.role: U.S. Senator from Rhode Island; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Promoting Responsible Managed Care Act of 1998 and delivered introductory remarks on it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over health insurance tax and ERISA provisions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on July 31, 1998, and never held a hearing or markup or reported it out; its history shows no action after the referral.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Did not bring the bill to the floor; in 1998 the Senate's leadership pursued narrower managed-care legislation instead of comprehensive patient-protection bills, and no comprehensive Senate patients' bill of rights came to a vote that year.

sides.party_line_note: The bill itself was bipartisan — sponsored by a Republican with three Democrats and one Republican cosponsor — but the Senate never moved it, and the broader 1998 fight over patient protections split largely along party lines, with Republican leadership favoring narrower legislation.

industries.industry: Managed care plans and health insurers
industries.note: The bill subjects them to detailed federal standards: mandatory appeal timelines, independent external review at their expense, disclosure of incentives and quality data, penalties, and liability for improper coverage determinations. Their gain from the bill's death is the continuation of the opaque utilization-review and denial practices the bill targeted.

ERISA plans would have had to comply with the patient-protection standards for the first time and plan fiduciaries could face civil penalties and economic-loss liability. Many employers opposed federal mandates on their health plans, and blocking the bill preserved that discretion.

industries.industry: Physicians and other health care providers
industries.note: The bill bans gag clauses, protects doctors who advocate for patients or support expedited appeals, restricts physician incentive plans tied to denying care, and gives providers standing in coverage determinations and appeals.

industries.industry: Independent external review and accreditation entities
industries.note: The bill creates a market of qualified external appeal entities that every plan and issuer would have to contract with, plus federally funded Health Insurance Ombudsman organizations to counsel consumers.
